claims.text: incident-response.md lines 3-7: in use from stage-4, drilled on staging with incident-drill.sh; every time in the file is an assumption. Lines 11-12: the level follows impact on customers, not the cause; on-call sets it when acknowledging the page and changes it when impact changes.

Table l.14-18: SEV1 all shops' orders fail -> on-call+lead, PO tells shops, 30 min; SEV2 page alert of S2-S4 or partial S1 -> on-call, more if needed, 60 min if customers see it; SEV3 ticket alert -> nobody called, nothing sent. Rule label: page = call on-call now, ticket = working-hours work.
claims.source_hint: docs/team/incident-response.md lines 14-18; docs/design/alerts.md lines 62-65 at stage-4

claims.text: SLIs: S1 orders placed without 5xx, S2 orders placed within the latency bucket, S3 product reads without 5xx, S4 refund requests within the bucket. ProductReadsFastBurn is the severity: page alert of S3, so it is SEV2 under the table.
claims.source_hint: docs/design/slo.md lines 24-27; docs/design/alerts.md line 57; incident-response.md line 17 at stage-4

claims.text: Roles (l.20-28): commander decides what is tried next and who does it, keeps the timeline, calls more people, does not debug (doing both loses the overall picture); responder follows runbook and assigned work; communications writes shop updates via the product owner (who tells shops, l.16).

Lines 30-33: on-call holds command from acknowledging the page until an explicit handover in words; with one person deciding, two people do not make conflicting changes, such as a commit revert while another edits the same Deployment by hand.
Prometheus holds alert state (pending, firing) but sends no notification itself; staging runs no notifier, so the person on-call sees an alert by looking at staging's Prometheus.
claims.source_hint: Prometheus docs, Alerting overview (alerts go to an Alertmanager); docs/team/on-call.md lines 89-98 at stage-4

claims.text: Lines 35-38: in a team of four, SEV2 often has only the on-call, who holds all three roles; a second person -> split command off first; SEV1 always separates at least commander and responder; team lead or product owner takes communications.

Shop updates (lines 40-50): shops' words, three parts (since when and what they see; what the team does; next update time), no guessed cause; cause stated once certain, a wrong one sent must be retracted and costs trust.

Timeline (lines 52-65): commander or delegate records what was seen, decided and done, each with a time; the example (lines 58-61) follows the drill's fault with assumed times, 10:02 firing to 10:15 alert gone; memory afterwards is incomplete and out of order, the review is written from it.

End (lines 69-71): incident ends when the alert has resolved and the SLI stays good for 30 minutes (assumed) with the mitigation in place, not when the cause is known; the commander declares the end, communications sends a final update.
Lines 73-75 and slo.md: an incident spending more than a quarter of an SLI's error budget requires a written review within five working days; smaller ones may get one too.
claims.source_hint: docs/team/incident-response.md lines 73-75; docs/design/slo.md line 95 at stage-4

claims.text: Drill output: ProductReadsFastBurn pending then firing with both shares above 6.7%, the newest envs/staging commit reverted, then inactive.

When two or more people respond, one commander who does not debug fits; one person holding every role fits only when one person responds; nobody leading rarely fits, so command is split off when a second person joins.

Scheduled updates without a cause fit when customers can see the problem (SEV1, SEV2). When they cannot (SEV3, staging), the file sends shops nothing at all. An early guess rarely fits: a cause is stated once certain.

Choices: night SEV2 alone -> hold all roles, keep timeline, update only if customers see it; SEV1 with team lead -> stay commander unless handed over, call a responder, lead/PO on communications every 30 min; alert resolved, cause unknown -> end after SLI good for the agreed time.
If the senior engineer wants to debug, they work as a responder while the person on-call commands; if they take command, they stop debugging.
